summary: New Dorp Light, a wooden range light on Staten Island, was built in the mid-1850s for the Swash Channel range. The Coast Guard decommissioned it in 1964; it is privately owned.

lens.note: Original second-order range lens (LighthouseFriends); sixth-order range lens installed 1939 (LighthouseFriends; U.S. Lighthouse Society record gives the current optic as sixth order, range).

structures.note: Square tower rising from the centre of the keeper's dwelling; 40 ft (12.2 m) to lantern centre (U.S. Lighthouse Society). The 1967 landmark report gives 'about 1854' as the building date.

access.note: Privately owned. Grounds, dwelling and tower closed (LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: Private owner since 1974 (LighthouseFriends). New York City landmark since 1967 (landmarks designation LP-0361).

events.note: Built about 1854 according to the 1967 landmark report; the same report gives 1856 for establishment
Contract dated 11 June 1855 for six range beacons, to be finished by 25 October 1855 (LighthouseFriends)
Station established; original range lens installed (U.S. Lighthouse Society)
Discontinued as a war measure on 28 April 1898
Light source changed from oil to incandescent oil vapor (LighthouseFriends)
New Dorp beacon of the Swash Channel range changed from incandescent oil vapor to electric incandescent
Station passed from the federal Lighthouse Service to the Coast Guard
Sixth-order range lens installed, showing a fixed white light (LighthouseFriends)
Decommissioned by the Coast Guard on 15 June 1964; light darkened; house windows boarded up
Designated a New York City landmark, LP-0361, on 15 November 1967
Sold at auction to a Staten Island resident for $32,000 (LighthouseFriends)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1967 landmark report says 'built about 1854' and 'established in 1856'. The U.S. Lighthouse Society gives 1856 for the tower and keeper's quarters. The story reports the disagreement; it is not resolved.

notes_for_editor: NOT VERIFIED: The NRHP nomination for 73001260 is not digitised (npgallery returned a placeholder), so the 1973 NRHP listing from the station record is not footnoted or used in the story. The Wikipedia lead gives Congress's funding approval as 31 August 1852; Wikipedia is a lead only and that date is not used. The 1855 Board report and the Board's 1855-1856 annual reports are not in the local corpus. Build date conflict: 1852 funds (Wikipedia, lead only), 1854 (1967 landmark report), 1855 contract and October 1855 completion (LighthouseFriends), 1856 (U.S. Lighthouse Society; landmark report 'established'). LighthouseFriends spells the builder Calrow (the story keeps that spelling). Search snippets for other sites (not read) give Carlow; that is unverified and not used. LighthouseFriends spells the keeper Langston; the archive roster has Langton. The story uses the roster spelling. Margaret J. Langston's death in February 1896 (LighthouseFriends, citing The Press, 10 February 1896) is not used: the newspaper was not found in the search and the detail concerns a minor. The 1922 'New Dorp ghost' article (LighthouseFriends) was not traced. A 1922 Evening World search returned unrelated items. The story attributes the claim to LighthouseFriends. The 1939 transfer and 1964 decommissioning are from the 1967 landmark report; LighthouseFriends gives the same year for abandonment. Private owner: the 1974 buyer is a private person and is not named, per the guidance on private residents. Roster: the archive lists 'Charles Jones (1959-)' with no end date; the story gives the year only. Person slugs are from roster.py --json. No wrecks at the station are recorded in the sources read; the Swash Channel stranding lists in the Life-Saving Service reports name the channel, not this station, and are not used. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-27: The 1899 Board report (scan p. 108) lists several lower-bay lights as discontinued on 28 April 1898 as a war measure (among them Point Comfort, Conover, Elm Tree and Fort Tompkins); the story names Point Comfort and Conover. The 1924 Bulletin has two listings of the Swash Channel change: PDF p. 14 (Elm Tree and New Dorp beacons, incandescent oil vapor to electric incandescent) and PDF p. 32 (Swash Channel Range, oil to electric incandescent, two lights). The story states both and the disagreement. LighthouseFriends says a contract was entered into on 11 June 1855; it does not say the Board signed it, and the story does not say so. The Olsen 1867 line is the archive's; the story says only that the roster lists him for 1867. The LighthouseFriends right-of-way quotation is paraphrased. The Spanish-American War context sentence was removed as uncited general context. The status of the 1922 article is not repeated in the story; it stays here. Charles Jones (from 1959) is named only as the archive prints him, with no personal detail.
